newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistani leaders vow to fight violence.
newsitem.headline: Pakistani leaders vow to fight violence.

text.p: Pakistani leaders vowed on Friday to fight spreading religious and ethnic violence which they said was fanned from outside the country.

"A handful of people are fanning sectarianism in the name of Islam at the behest of foreign elements, but we will bring peace in the country at all costs," Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif said in a speech to a conference to mark the birthday of Islam's prophet Mohammad.

President Farooq Leghari, speaking at the same conference, said sectarian violence had reached "such a proportion that people are being killed in streets, bazaars and mosques" in what he called s conspiracy to damage Pakistan's Islamic ideology.
Pakistan has seen a resurgence of ethnic violence in the southern city of Karachi and sectarian violence in Punjab province.
Punjab Chief Minister Shahbaz Sharif, the brother of the prime minister, threatened in a speech in the provincial capital Lahore to act against religious schools that were training "murderers".

More than 100 people, including religious scholars, lawyers and doctors, have been killed in Punjab this year in attacks blamed on each other by rival groups of the majority Sunni and the minority Shi'ite sects of Islam.
In Karachi, police say more than 160 people have been killed in political violence since March compared to 500 in 1996 and more than 2,000 in 1995.
Three bodies, two of them strangled, were recovered from different areas of Karachi on Friday, police said.
"The problems of sectarianism, linguistic differences and terrorism faced by Pakistan today cannot be resolved by the government alone," Leghari said in a message to mark the prophet's birthday.
"The entire nation should help the government to find out its causes and remedies."
Shahbaz Sharif said Pakistan had never faced a situation in which activists of rival religious factions killed each other to "achieve a place in Paradise".
Shi'ites form about 15 percent of Pakistan's mainly Sunni population of more than 135 million but are the majority in neighbouring Iran.
